title: Books With Missing Letters
description: Gadsby's missing E, Perec's vanishing novel La Disparition, and Eunoia's one-vowel chapters

concepts.title: Gadsby: 50,000 Words Without an E
concepts.contentHtml:
The title page makes the promise: Gadsby, published in 1939, is a story of over 50,000 words written without the letter E. Its author, Ernest Vincent Wright, explained in his introduction how he kept himself honest. The whole manuscript was typed with the E type-bar of his typewriter tied down, so that no stray E could sneak in.1

Why bother? Wright said someone had told him that coherent, grammatical English could not be written without its most common letter, and he set out, apparently in 1936–37, to prove them wrong.2

The price was steep. Without E there is no the, no he, she or they, no past tense ending in -ed and no number from six to thirty. The story itself is a sunny small-town tale: John Gadsby comes home to the run-down town of Branton Hills, rallies its young people to revive it, and by the end the population has grown thirtyfold and he is mayor. Wright did not quite reach perfection, either: three stray thes and an officer slipped into the first printing. Self-published to no fanfare, the book is now far more often cited as a piece of trivia than actually read.3

For decades it was hard even to find. In 1988 the wordplay journal Word Ways called it one of those books that many people have heard about but few have seen, and noted that a copy in its dust jacket had once sold for $1,000.4 The joke is that the stunt works. A whole novel without E is perfectly possible; it just comes out a little stiff, like a man walking carefully around a hole in the floor.

concepts.title: La Disparition: A Novel About What Is Missing
concepts.contentHtml:
Thirty years later a French writer went further. Georges Perec's La Disparition ("The Disappearance", 1969) is a 300-page novel in which no word contains the letter E. Perec had joined the Oulipo two years earlier, a group of writers who set themselves strict rules to work under. The plot is itself a disappearance. A man named Anton Voyl vanishes, and as his friends search his writings for clues, each one dies just as he is about to say a word containing E.1

The book is full of hints at what is missing. Its chapters run from 1 to 26, as many as there are letters, but there is no chapter five, and E is the fifth letter. Even the hero's name is a clue: in English, Anton Voyl becomes Anton Vowl. The Oulipians once described themselves as rats who must build the labyrinth from which they propose to escape, and Perec's maze is also a spoof of a detective story.2

Translating it looked impossible. The Scottish writer Gilbert Adair at first turned the job down, then started in 1990, and four years later published A Void, an English version that also never uses E.3 A literal title would have failed: The Disappearance breaks the rule three times.

Under the game lies a real absence. Perec's father was killed at the front in 1940, and his mother was deported to Auschwitz.4 The scholar Priya Wadhera reads the novel as a silent protest: the missing e is meant to evoke the lack of eux, French for "them", those who perished in the Holocaust, including Perec's own mother.5 A book that never says the word for mother (mère has an E in it) is, in the end, about the people who are not there.

concepts.title: Eunoia: One Vowel per Chapter
concepts.contentHtml:
"Writing is inhibiting. Sighing, I sit, scribbling in ink this pidgin script."1 Every word there has I as its only vowel, and so does every word in the rest of "Chapter I".

It comes from Eunoia (2001) by the Canadian poet Christian Bök, a five-chapter book in which each chapter is a univocal lipogram: the first uses only the vowel A, the second only E, and so on. The title, meaning "beautiful thinking", is the shortest English word that contains all five vowels. Each vowel takes on a personality: I is egotistical and romantic, O jocular and obscene, E elegiac and epic, with a retelling of the Iliad. The book won the 2002 Griffin Poetry Prize and became a bestseller in Canada and Britain.2

Bök piled on extra rules. Every chapter alludes to the art of writing and describes a banquet, a scene of debauchery and a nautical voyage, and he also did without the letter Y, which can stand in for a vowel.3

Finding the words was the hard part. Bök read all three volumes of Webster's Third International Unabridged Dictionary five times, pulling out every word with only one of the five vowels. He sorted them into parts of speech and topics to see what stories each vowel could tell, then spent six years, four or five hours a night from about midnight, fitting them together. He began to feel "that language played host to a conspiracy".4

"When I began, I thought it would only take six months," he told students in 2002. In all, Eunoia took seven years, and once it was finished, publishers were reluctant to take it on.5 The rule that looked like a cage had worked as an engine.

title: Hoaxes That Fooled Critics
description: Ern Malley's fake poems, a sex novel written badly on purpose, and the Atlanta Nights sting

concepts.title: Ern Malley, the Poet Who Never Was
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1943 Max Harris, the 22-year-old editor of the Melbourne-based modernist journal Angry Penguins, got a letter from Ethel Malley, who had found poems among her late brother's things. Ern Malley, a mechanic and insurance salesman, had died young of Graves' disease, and Harris was sure he was an undiscovered genius. The June 1944 issue printed all of it, 35 pages titled "The Darkening Ecliptic", with a cover by Sidney Nolan. Then Sydney's Sunday Sun revealed on its front page that Ern Malley had never existed.1

He was the invention of James McAuley and Harold Stewart, two young poets who disliked modernism. They wanted to see whether Harris could tell "a collection of garish images without coherent meaning and structure" from the real thing.2 Both were soldiers, and they wrote Ern's whole life's work in one afternoon at the Victoria Barracks in Melbourne. The rule was that every word had to come from the books in front of them: Shakespeare, the Concise Oxford Dictionary, a dictionary of quotations, a pocket rhyming dictionary and a manual on mosquito control.

Worse followed. In September 1944 the South Australian police prosecuted Harris under the Indecent Advertisements Act. The detective objected to the word "incestuous": "I don't know what that means but I think there is a suggestion of indecency about it." Harris argued the poems were no more suggestive than Chaucer or Shakespeare, but he was fined £5.3

Yet the joke never fully landed. Many readers insisted they enjoyed the poems, arguing that the hoaxers had accidentally written better verse than they managed when trying to be serious.4 The poet John Tranter, who later devoted an issue of his magazine Jacket to the affair, says the hoax inspired the American poet John Ashbery as a young man.5

concepts.title: Naked Came the Stranger: Bad on Purpose
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1966 Mike McGrady, a columnist at the Long Island newspaper Newsday, decided to test a theory: that American taste had sunk so low that a book with no merit at all would sell, as long as it was packed with sex. He gave his colleagues an outline and a warning: "True excellence in writing will be blue-penciled into oblivion. There will be an unremitting emphasis on sex."1

Volunteers each wrote a chapter of at least 2,500 words. The heroine, Gillian Blake, is half of a husband-and-wife radio team; when she learns her husband is cheating, she takes revenge by breaking up every marriage in her community. The team meant to finish in a week and took a year. McGrady and his colleague Harvey Aronson did the editing, and McGrady's sister-in-law, the right age and a look-alike for the best-selling Jacqueline Susann, posed as the author, "Penelope Ashe". Columbia University, which holds McGrady's papers, counts 26 reporters in all.2

Published in 1969, the novel had sold a respectable 20,000 copies when, on August 6, the reporters revealed they were the real authors. Instead of killing the book, the confession sold far more copies.3 By November 2, 1969, it stood at No. 3 on the New York Times best-seller list, though that paper had reviewed it in August without spotting the parody.4

So the experiment proved McGrady's point twice over. Reception was mixed, but many people thought the hoax a clever ruse and still liked the book. A year later McGrady told the whole story in Stranger Than Naked, or How to Write Dirty Books for Fun and Profit.5

concepts.title: Atlanta Nights: Stinging a Vanity Press
concepts.contentHtml:
PublishAmerica claimed to be a serious "traditional publisher", one that chose its books and held them to editorial standards. Critics called it a vanity press. So a group of science fiction and fantasy writers, organized by James D. Macdonald, set out to test the claim with the worst novel they could manage.

Some thirty authors each banged out a chapter or two over a long weekend, from a brief outline and a few character notes. Nobody knew what was in the other chapters, or even where theirs would fall in the book. Macdonald's account even echoes McGrady's memo of 1966: "Any accidental literary competence was rapidly blue-penciled into oblivion."1

The result was gloriously broken. Chapter 21 is missing, replaced by a second chapter 12; chapter 4 appears again, word for word, as chapter 17; and chapter 34 was generated entirely by a computer program.2 Characters change sex, or die and reappear without explanation, and at one point everything so far turns out to have been a dream, after which the book carries on for several more chapters. The byline, Travis Tea, is a pun on "travesty".3

PublishAmerica accepted Atlanta Nights. On legal advice, the authors revealed the hoax before signing a contract that would have guaranteed the book was written solely by its named author, and PublishAmerica backed out.4 The writers then published it themselves through Lulu.com, with the proceeds going to an emergency medical fund for science fiction writers.5 The sting had made its point: a publisher that claimed to select its books had said yes to one whose chapters repeat, vanish and contradict each other.

title: Authors Who Weren't
description: Romain Gary's second Goncourt as Émile Ajar, the JT LeRoy persona, and Helen Demidenko

concepts.title: The Man Who Won the Goncourt Twice
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1975 France's top literary prize, the Prix Goncourt, went to La Vie devant soi, a novel by an unknown writer named Émile Ajar. Literary Paris wanted to know who he was. The publisher said the manuscripts had arrived by mail. Some critics suspected the novelist Romain Gary, who issued a statement denying any connection, and then a man named Paul Pavlowitch announced that he was Ajar.1

The suspicious critics were right. Gary had already won the Goncourt in 1956, for Les Racines du ciel.2 By the 1970s the writer and film director had grown, in his own words, "tired of being nothing but myself," so he invented someone else to be.3 But the Goncourt is awarded to an author only once, and the win shone a spotlight on an author who did not exist. So Gary got his cousin's son, Pavlowitch, to play the part of Ajar in public.4

The secret held for the rest of Gary's life. He took his own life in December 1980, and in July 1981 Pavlowitch published a memoir saying that Gary had written La Vie devant soi and three other Ajar novels, and had asked him to pose as their author.5

The hoax worked because readers judge a book partly by the name on its cover. As "Romain Gary" he was an established author with a settled reputation; as "Émile Ajar" the same writer was judged as an unknown newcomer, and the jury that could never knowingly give him a second Goncourt gave him one anyway.

concepts.title: The Writer in the Wig: JT LeRoy
concepts.contentHtml:
Around 2000, one of the most talked-about young writers in America was a teenager almost nobody had seen clearly. JT LeRoy's life was said to be as harrowing as his fiction: a truck-stop prostitute who had escaped rural West Virginia, only to end up homeless and addicted in San Francisco, until a couple named Laura Albert and Geoffrey Knoop took him in and he began to write. His three books of fiction won critical acclaim.1

The story began to come apart in October 2005, when New York magazine published a theory that Laura Albert herself was the author.2 In January 2006 the New York Times reported that the shy young man in the wig and sunglasses who appeared in public was not a man at all. The public JT LeRoy was Savannah Knoop, Geoffrey Knoop's half-sibling.3

The name had also been used to sign contracts, and that brought the case to court. In June 2007 a federal jury in Manhattan found that Albert had committed fraud and breach of contract by signing an option on the film rights to her novel Sarah (2000) as LeRoy, and ordered her to pay $116,500 to the production company, Antidote International Films.4

Albert rejects the word hoax. In the 2016 documentary Author: The JT LeRoy Story she traces the persona to a childhood of abuse and instability and insists that LeRoy was an "avatar" that let her write prose she could not produce in her own voice.5 Whatever one calls it, the case left readers with an awkward question: had they been moved by the books, or by the story of the boy who was supposed to have written them?

concepts.title: Helen Demidenko's Invented Past
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1993 a young writer won the Vogel award, a prize for unpublished manuscripts, with a novel called The Hand That Signed the Paper. It presented itself as a family history built on oral testimony, about a Ukrainian family's part in the Holocaust. Its author called herself Helen Demidenko and claimed Irish-Ukrainian ancestry, and that background was central to the judges' belief that the book was authentic. She dressed the part too, often wearing Ukrainian peasant blouses to literary events. In 1995 the novel won the prestigious Miles Franklin Award.1

The book was controversial from the start. Its central character, Vitaly, is a Ukrainian war criminal living in Australia who explains his part in the mass killing of Jews by pointing to Jewish involvement in Russian rule over Ukraine. Defenders said a novel is not history; critics said it distorted the history of Ukrainian-Jewish relations and offered a justification of genocide.2

Then, in August 1995, newspapers looked into the author. They reported that her parents were Harry and Grace Darville, migrants from the north of England, though she had claimed her father was an illiterate Ukrainian taxi driver. Her father told a reporter that he and his wife were proud she had won the Miles Franklin.3 The novel was reissued that year under her real name, Helen Darville.4

Why did the name matter so much? Michael Heyward, the historian of Australia's Ern Malley hoax, argued that by becoming her own creation, Darville made Helen Demidenko real, and that in turn made the events in the book seem real.5 The prize juries had partly been rewarding testimony, and the testimony was invented.

title: Unfinished, Unreadable, Unproven
description: Dickens's unfinished Drood, the unreadable Codex Seraphinianus, and Hemingway's baby shoes

concepts.title: Who Killed Edwin Drood?
concepts.contentHtml:
Charles Dickens died halfway through a murder mystery. The Mystery of Edwin Drood was planned as twelve monthly installments, and he had completed six when he died, leaving the second half of the story unknown. What survives sets up the crime and stops: young Edwin Drood disappears, and the reader already knows that his uncle, John Jasper, secretly loves Edwin's fiancée, Rosa Bud.1

Was Edwin even dead? Hints passed on by people close to Dickens suggest that Jasper was meant to strangle Edwin with a scarf and hide the body in quicklime. Yet Dickens also jotted down possible titles such as "The Flight of Edwin Drood" and "Edwin Drood in Hiding", so he may at least have considered letting Edwin live. Nobody can know, which has not stopped dozens of writers from finishing the book themselves.2

Readers have also put the case on trial. Forty-four years after Dickens's death in 1870, the Dickens Fellowship charged Jasper, an opium addict, with murder. At the mock trial on 7 January 1914, G. K. Chesterton sat as judge and George Bernard Shaw was foreman of the jury.3 Shaw announced a compromise. Some jurors had wanted to acquit, since there was no evidence that a murder had happened at all; others feared that freeing Jasper would get everyone murdered in their beds. So they found him guilty of manslaughter.4

The puzzle still fills theaters. In 1985 the composer Rupert Holmes turned it into a Broadway musical in which the audience votes on who killed Edwin Drood, if anyone did. At one early performance the audience elected sweet Rosa Bud the murderer.5 With no official ending, every reader's solution is as good as the next.

concepts.title: The Encyclopedia Nobody Can Read
concepts.contentHtml:
Picture an encyclopedia of another world. Page after page shows strange plants, animals, machines and buildings, in dreamlike drawings, and every caption, label and paragraph is written in a flowing, made-up script. That is the Codex Seraphinianus, a book of about 360 pages by the Italian artist and designer Luigi Serafini, first published in 1981.1

Readers took it as a challenge. Language scholars and amateurs alike have tried to decipher the text, and everyone has failed; only the page numbers have been worked out.2 In a 2004 analysis Ivan Derzhanski showed that they are written, on the whole, in base 21, with twenty-one digits running from 0 to 20.3

Serafini says there is nothing else to find. Asked in 2013 about a blogger who claimed to have cracked the Codex, he said: "I always said that there is no meaning behind the script; it's just a game."4

So why does decoding go on? The script is regular enough to look like a language, with repeated shapes and counted pages, and that is all a pattern-hungry brain needs. The writer Alberto Manguel puts it more grandly: "We have a tendency to believe that everything that surrounds us is an encoded language."5 The Codex may be best read as a test of that tendency rather than a message waiting for its key.

concepts.title: The Six-Word Story Hemingway Didn't Write
concepts.contentHtml:
"For sale: baby shoes, never worn." Six words in the shape of a classified ad, and a whole tragedy opens up behind them. The famous story is that Ernest Hemingway wrote them to win a bet with other writers, but the fact-checking site Snopes rates that claim false.1 Quote Investigator, which traces quotations to their earliest sources, found no substantive evidence that Hemingway wrote the line. He died in 1961, and the oldest known account of the bet comes from a literary agent, Peter Miller, who said a newspaper syndicator told it to him around 1974 and who published it in a 1991 book.2

The idea itself is older than the legend. Real small ads like it appeared in newspapers over the decades; one printed in 1906 read "For sale, baby carriage; never been used." In 1910 a newspaper turned a similar ad, for a baby's clothes and bed that had never been used, into a short article about a family's grief. And in 1917 William R. Kane, writing for authors, suggested "Little Shoes, Never Worn" as the title for a story about a wife who has lost her baby.3

Hemingway's name arrives very late. The earliest printed version known to Quote Investigator that puts the line in his mouth is a one-man play about him, Papa by John De Groot, released in 1989, nearly thirty years after his death.4 The pattern is a common one for quotations: a line that circulates without an author drifts toward a famous name that seems to fit it, and Hemingway, the master of the short, plain sentence, fit it perfectly.
